records.name: Australia

skilled_routes.name: Skills in Demand visa (subclass 482, Core Skills stream)
skilled_routes.summary: Employer-sponsored 4-year work visa; leads to permanent Employer Nomination Scheme (186) after 2 years with the sponsor. Software roles qualify on the Core Skills Occupation List.
skilled_routes.threshold_note: CSIT AUD 79,423 from 1 Jul 2026 (indexed +3.9%); Specialist Skills stream (SSIT) AUD 146,576 = ~USD 102,800 skips occupation lists

skilled_routes.name: Skilled Independent / State Nominated (189/190/491)
skilled_routes.summary: Points-tested permanent residence via SkillSelect EOI. A leaked 2025 FOI tier model puts ICT occupations in the lowest-priority Tier 4, so software applicants realistically need very high points (roughly 85-95 in recent rounds) or state nomination (190/491) rather than the formal 65-point minimum.
skilled_routes.threshold_note: No salary threshold; points-based. ICT = Tier 4 (lowest invitation priority) per May-2025 FOI minute

study_pathway.note: Typical international CS master's AUD 40k-52k/yr at public unis (midpoint AUD 46k used; estimate). Temporary Graduate 485 Post-Higher-Education stream: 2 yrs for bachelor/master (3 for research/PhD), age <35; application fee doubled to AUD 4,600 on 1 Mar 2026 - world's most expensive post-study visa.

iran_friction.notes: Iranian applicants routinely face multi-year external security checks on 485/189/190; in July 2026 Home Affairs declined to give any timeline for delayed Iranian skilled-visa cases (Iran International). Student visas are granted but with elevated scrutiny and high evidentiary bars; sanctions banking complicates fee payment and fund transfers from Iran. Community reporting shows 1-3 year waits on PR-track grants for Iranian nationals.

dual_citizenship.note: Dual citizenship permitted since 2002; no renunciation required, so Iran's non-recognition of renunciation creates no issue.

tax.summary: Progressive income tax (top 45% + 2% Medicare); no employee social security, but employer pays ~12% superannuation on top of salary.
tax.net_note: ~AUD 110,000 mid-level dev salary; 2025-26 ATO resident rates + 2% Medicare, own computation (net ~AUD 84,000)

indices.freedom_note: Australia is a stable liberal democracy with marriage equality (since 2017) and strong formal protections, but there is no federal ban on LGBTQ+ conversion practices, a 2026 hate-speech law reform left LGBTQIA+ protections largely unaddressed, and asylum-seeker policy has hardened further, including a 2026 forced-deportation arrangement with Nauru struck after courts ruled indefinite detention illegal.

job_market.summary: Australia's tech sector is large (A$167 billion) but 2026 hiring has clearly cooled: national job ads were down about 5% in February 2026, and tech-specific layoffs jumped from 874 in all of 2025 to over 4,450 in early 2026 alone, including WiseTech Global cutting 30% of staff and Atlassian cutting roughly 1,600 roles. Sydney posted around 3,600 tech layoffs in 2026, the third-highest of any city globally after Seattle and San Francisco. Demand has shifted away from generalist software development toward cybersecurity, cloud, data/AI, and platform engineering; Sydney and Melbourne are the dominant hubs, with Brisbane, Canberra, Adelaide, and Perth smaller markets.
job_market.new_grad_reality: Genuinely hard and getting harder: recruiters report shrinking entry-level roles as AI absorbs junior tasks, competition averages around 185 applicants per IT role, and hiring now takes 8-10 weeks instead of 5-6. For a foreign new grad with no local network or existing work rights, a first dev job typically means a long, multi-month search.

language.official: English (no legally declared official language, but English is the de facto language of government, education, and all visa/citizenship testing)
language.pr_citizenship_language_req: Citizenship applicants generally must demonstrate 'competent English' (similar to the points-tested skilled-visa standard) and pass a citizenship test delivered in English (75%+ to pass; a 2025-2026 reform added assessed writing, listening and speaking). Passport holders from the UK, US, Canada, NZ or Ireland are exempt from separate English testing - an exemption that does not extend to Iranian nationals. This area is under active reform; verify current specifics on the Department of Home Affairs site.

records.reality_paragraph: For a skilled migrant, Australia offers a genuinely high standard of living, a strong work-life-balance culture, and Medicare once you have PR - but 2026 is a cooler year for tech hiring than usual, and housing is the biggest financial shock: Sydney's median dwelling price is around A$1.3 million and renting a typical house there now takes roughly A$135,000/year in income to avoid 'rental stress'; Melbourne is somewhat more affordable but still tight. Integration is generally logistically smooth - English-speaking, Western institutions, an established multicultural population - but diaspora and academic research paint a more mixed social picture: interviews with Iranian-Australian women describe workplace discrimination compounded by Islamophobia, while other research suggests more recently arrived, secular-leaning Iranian migrants in Sydney report less day-to-day racism than more religious or refugee-background arrivals, suggesting experience depends heavily on background. Australia's Iranian community is smaller than the US or Canada's - about 71,000 Iran-born residents (2021 Census), concentrated in Sydney (~26,000) and Melbourne (~21,000) - and about 12.4% of Iran-born Australians report not speaking English well, pointing to a real settlement gap for some arrivals even though skilled migrants themselves usually arrive fluent. There's no Iran-specific travel ban comparable to the US's, but Australia expelled Iran's ambassador in 2024 after attributing antisemitic attacks on Australian soil to the Iranian state, which can mean extra security scrutiny for Iranian nationals. A commonly cited regret is underestimating how long and expensive it is to buy property, plus the isolation of a long, costly flight from family; what people love is the lifestyle trade-off - shorter effective work weeks, outdoor living, and a less frantic professional culture.

records.name: United States

skilled_routes.name: H-1B (specialty occupation)
skilled_routes.summary: Employer-petitioned, cap-subject (85k/yr). Registrations vastly exceed the cap (FY2024: 758,994 registrations for 110,791 selections); from 27 Feb 2026 selection is wage-level-weighted (Level IV entered 4x, Level I once), disadvantaging new grads. The Sept 2025 $100,000 supplemental fee proclamation was voided by a federal judge on 8 Jun 2026 (litigation ongoing).
skilled_routes.threshold_note: No fixed statutory minimum; DOL prevailing wage by occupation/area governs, and low wage levels now rarely win the weighted lottery

skilled_routes.name: O-1A (extraordinary ability)
skilled_routes.summary: Uncapped employer/agent-petitioned route for individuals with sustained acclaim (publications, awards, critical roles); increasingly used by elite engineers/founders. No lottery, premium processing available - but consular issuance is blocked for Iranian nationals under the travel ban.
skilled_routes.threshold_note: No salary threshold; evidence-based standard

study_pathway.note: Public-university international MS tuition typically $30k-55k/yr (privates higher); estimate $40k. F-1 OPT 12 months + 24-month STEM extension = 36 months for CS. Caveat: new F-1 visas are currently not issued to single-nationality Iranians under Proclamation 10949.

iran_friction.notes: Proclamation 10949 (in force 9 Jun 2025) fully suspends immigrant and nonimmigrant entry of Iranian nationals; Proclamation 10998 (eff. 1 Jan 2026) expanded the ban to 39 countries and removed the adoption/immediate-relative exceptions. Exemptions cover existing visa holders, green-card holders, dual nationals using a non-banned passport, persecuted religious/ethnic minorities (immigrant visas) and major sports events. Practically: no new F-1/H-1B/O-1 visas for most Iranians while the ban stands; change of status inside the US remains possible.

dual_citizenship.note: US tolerates dual citizenship; naturalization oath is not enforced as renunciation, so Iranian nationality can be retained.

tax.summary: Federal progressive tax (10-37%) + 7.65% FICA + state income tax (0-13% depending on state).
tax.net_note: $120,000 mid-level dev salary, single filer, 2026 federal brackets + FICA + ~5% average state tax, own computation (SmartAsset-style); ranges ~66% (CA/NY) to ~77% (TX/WA)

indices.freedom_note: The US remains a rule-of-law democracy with strong formal free-speech and press protections, but LGBTQ+ rights and the lived social climate now vary sharply by state and have grown more polarized - 2025 alone saw anti-LGBTQ legislative action in at least 22 states against pro-LGBTQ action in only 14 - so whether the US feels accepting depends heavily on which state and community you land in.

job_market.summary: US tech layoffs remain severe in 2026 - over 117,000 tech jobs cut so far this year, including Microsoft (15,000+) and Oracle (20,000-30,000) - even as companies keep hiring for AI-related and senior roles. Main hubs remain the SF Bay Area, Seattle, New York, and Austin, though some hiring is dispersing toward lower-cost metros. The long-run outlook is still positive on paper (BLS projects +15% software-developer growth through 2034), but that's little comfort for anyone job-hunting in 2026 itself.
job_market.new_grad_reality: Genuinely brutal, and worse specifically for foreign grads: entry-level postings have shrunk to roughly 7.5% of listings, new grads now make up only ~7% of Big Tech hires (down over 50% from 2019), and only 44.6% of international students land a US job after graduating versus 62.1% of domestic peers. The new wage-weighted H-1B lottery (effective February 2026) gives entry-level applicants only about a 15% selection chance versus roughly 61% for senior roles, so even a job offer doesn't guarantee a visa.

language.official: English (no federally declared official language, but the de facto language of government and business, and a core naturalization requirement)
language.pr_citizenship_language_req: Naturalization requires passing an English test (reading, writing, speaking) plus a civics test, with narrow age/residency exemptions: applicants 50+ with 20 years as a permanent resident, or 55+ with 15 years, are exempt from the English test (still take civics with an interpreter); 65+ with 20 years get a simplified civics test in their native language. Most working-age skilled migrants face full English-plus-civics testing with no shortcut.

records.reality_paragraph: The US still offers the highest ceiling on tech compensation and the deepest concentration of cutting-edge employers of any country here, but 2026 is a genuinely hard year to break in, with layoffs topping 117,000 tech jobs and entry-level hiring the tightest part of the market. Cost of living in the major hubs is extreme: San Francisco rent has hit a record ~$3,827/month, and even Seattle - the relatively 'affordable' option - runs a median rent around $2,058-2,119/month. But the single most important fact for an Iranian national right now isn't economic: as of January 1, 2026, Presidential Proclamation 10998 suspends US visa issuance to Iranian nationals across nearly every immigrant and nonimmigrant category, including student and work visas, with only narrow exceptions (dual nationals on a non-restricted passport, persecuted religious/ethnic minorities, existing green-card/valid-visa holders). People who already held a valid visa before that date haven't had it revoked, but anyone applying fresh from Iran faces close to a categorical bar - this is a fast-moving, actively litigated policy area (last confirmed February 2026) and must be re-verified before relying on it. For the roughly 750,000-strong Iranian-American community - the largest, most institutionally developed Persian diaspora of any country here, concentrated in LA's 'Tehrangeles' (~230,000) with further hubs in Texas, New York, and DC - diaspora reporting describes real cultural infrastructure alongside notably strong socioeconomic outcomes (median Iranian-American household income around $97,000 vs. a national median of about $70,000), plus a persistent undercurrent of displacement described in diaspora writing as 'ghorbat.' A commonly cited regret is underestimating healthcare costs and the precarity of an employer-tied visa, since losing a job can mean losing legal status within months; what people love is the sheer career ceiling and speed of professional advancement at the top of the US market.

records.name: Canada

skilled_routes.name: Express Entry (FSW/CEC) + PNP
skilled_routes.summary: CRS-ranked pool with targeted draws. In 2025-26 there are no all-program draws: invitations go to CEC (Canadian experience), provincial nominees, French speakers and narrow categories - July 2026 CEC cutoffs were 516-517, French draws dipped below 400. Candidates abroad without Canadian experience or strong French have little realistic draw access; the practical route is study/work in Canada first (or a PNP employer job offer).
skilled_routes.threshold_note: No salary threshold; CRS points. Realistic 2026 cutoffs: CEC ~516, PNP ~700s (incl. +600 nomination), French <400

study_pathway.note: International master's typically CAD 20k-40k/yr at public universities (est. CAD 28k). PGWP up to 3 years; master's grads (programs >=8 months) qualify for the 3-year permit and university-degree grads are exempt from the field-of-study restrictions that apply to college programs; CLB 7 language proof required.

iran_friction.notes: No visa office or biometrics collection in Iran - applicants travel to Türkiye, Armenia, Georgia or the UAE. Iranian study-permit refusal rates have run roughly 40-60% in recent years, and files often sit in extended security screening well beyond service standards (IRCC itself reported rising work/study permit wait times in July 2026). 2026 also saw security-inadmissibility proceedings against Iranian STEM doctoral students over alleged dual-use research links. Express Entry itself is nationality-neutral and Canada has a large Iranian community.

dual_citizenship.note: Dual citizenship fully permitted; Iranian nationality retention is not an obstacle.

tax.summary: Federal + provincial progressive income tax plus CPP/EI contributions; overall burden moderate.
tax.net_note: CAD 100,000 mid-level dev (Ontario): federal+provincial tax, CPP/CPP2 and EI per 2025-26 rates, own computation (net ~CAD 73,000)

indices.freedom_note: Canada's federal legal protections for LGBTQ+ rights, press freedom, and civil liberties remain strong and largely unchanged, but the social climate has grown more contested as US-style polarization spills across the border into debates over trans rights and education, and a 2024 Quebec survey found roughly 1 in 3 LGBT respondents had experienced workplace discrimination - legal equality doesn't automatically mean uniform day-to-day comfort.

job_market.summary: Canadian tech hiring in 2026 is described by industry reports as being in 'steady recovery' - demand is strong for AI/ML, cybersecurity, data analytics, and cloud roles, and the Greater Toronto Area alone sees 8,700+ unique software-developer postings a year. Layoffs continue in pockets (e.g., roughly 250 roles cut at Arctic Wolf in 2026), and generalist software-development roles are comparatively crowded compared to specialized AI/cybersecurity skills. Toronto (and the wider Toronto-Waterloo corridor) is the dominant hub, with Vancouver, Montreal, and Ottawa as secondary centers.
job_market.new_grad_reality: Still difficult for a foreign new grad specifically: generalist developer roles are the most crowded part of the market, and employers frequently weight 'Canadian experience' and credential recognition, so international graduates without a local internship or co-op tend to face a longer search than domestic grads - though the overall climate is less brutal than the US's right now.

language.official: English and French (bilingual federation; English dominates business and tech outside Quebec and parts of eastern Ontario/New Brunswick)
language.pr_citizenship_language_req: Citizenship applicants aged 18-54 must prove Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) Level 4 in either English or French - a functional-intermediate speaking-and-listening standard - via an approved test, education credentials, or government language-training records. Applicants under 18 or over 54 are exempt from the language requirement, though a separate citizenship knowledge test is still generally required.

records.reality_paragraph: Canada offers a clearer, more predictable path from skilled migrant to permanent resident to citizen than the US's employer-dependent system, but 2026 tech hiring - while framed as 'steady recovery' - is still selective: AI/ML and cybersecurity skills command a real premium while generalist developer roles are comparatively crowded. Housing is the main financial strain: a one-bedroom in Toronto runs around C$2,150/month and requires roughly C$96,000/year in gross income to stay within the standard 30%-of-income guideline, Vancouver is worse (~C$2,495/month, ~C$104,000/year needed), and home-purchase prices in both cities (roughly C$1.0-1.2 million median) are out of reach for most new arrivals for years. Integration is generally regarded as smoother than the US's on paper - the immigration system is explicitly built around skilled economic migrants - and there's a large, multi-generational Iranian-Persian community (about 280,805 combined Iranian/Persian-origin per the 2021 Census, concentrated in Greater Toronto ~97,000 and Greater Vancouver ~46,000) with established businesses, media, and Persian-language services. That said, a survey of 600+ Iranian-Canadians by the Iranian Canadian Congress found 65% report personally experiencing discrimination - half in employment/business settings and over a quarter during air travel or airport security - linked partly to hostile international rhetoric toward Iran. Canada has no Iran-specific travel ban comparable to the US's, which makes it the more realistic of the two North American options for Iranian nationals in 2026. A commonly cited regret is underestimating the housing crunch and how 'Canadian experience' requirements slow down a job search that actually matches your qualifications; what people love is the more predictable, less precarious path to permanent status and accessible provincial healthcare once it kicks in.

records.name: United Kingdom

skilled_routes.name: Skilled Worker visa
skilled_routes.summary: Sponsored by a licensed employer for an RQF6+ role; salary must meet BOTH the general threshold and the occupation going rate. Leads to settlement (currently after 5 years - reform pending).
skilled_routes.threshold_note: GBP 41,700 general threshold (from 22 Jul 2025); new entrants (incl. recent grads/under-26) GBP 33,400 = ~USD 44,900; occupation going rates may be higher

skilled_routes.name: High Potential Individual / Graduate routes
skilled_routes.summary: HPI: 2-year unsponsored visa (3 for PhD) for graduates of top-ranked global universities. Graduate route: post-study, unsponsored (see study_pathway). Neither leads directly to settlement; both are bridges into Skilled Worker.
skilled_routes.threshold_note: No salary requirement

study_pathway.note: International CS master's typically GBP 22k-35k (est. GBP 28k). Graduate visa: 2 years if you apply on or before 31 Dec 2026; 18 months for applications from 1 Jan 2027; 3 years for PhDs (gov.uk, verified Aug 2026).

iran_friction.notes: Iranian nationals need ATAS clearance for many sensitive STEM postgraduate courses (including parts of CS/AI), adding weeks and refusal risk. UK visa biometrics are generally not available inside Iran, so applicants usually travel to a third country. Sanctions-related banking checks complicate tuition and maintenance-funds transfers. The routes themselves are nationality-neutral and the UK has a large Iranian community. Big caveat for planning: the 'earned settlement' reform is expected to lengthen standard ILR from 5 to ~10 years (baseline) with earn-back provisions, applied retrospectively - final rules due autumn 2026.

dual_citizenship.note: Dual citizenship fully permitted; no renunciation issue for Iranians.

tax.summary: Progressive income tax (20/40/45%) plus 8%/2% employee National Insurance.
tax.net_note: GBP 55,000 mid-level dev salary; 2025-26 HMRC rates (income tax + Class 1 NI), own computation (net ~GBP 42,460). Note: 5-to-10-year ILR reform pending

indices.freedom_note: The UK is rated 'Free' by Freedom House (92/100) with strong press freedom (around 18th of 180 countries in 2026) and full legal protection for LGBTQ+ people under the Equality Act 2010, but it is currently dealing with a real and rising climate of Islamophobic and religiously-motivated hate crime (sharply up since the 2024 Southport riots) and an increasingly contested political and legal fight over trans rights specifically.

job_market.summary: UK tech hiring in 2026 is best described as 'not a crash, a correction': vacancies are down roughly 18% from the late-2024 peak and entry-level/junior roles (especially frontend-only and manual QA) are genuinely contracting as AI tooling absorbs junior tasks, while cybersecurity, cloud/platform engineering, data engineering and AI-adjacent roles remain in strong, under-supplied demand. London remains the dominant hub, with secondary clusters growing in Manchester, Birmingham, Edinburgh, Bristol and Leeds. Contract/project-based hiring is gaining ground on permanent hiring as employers stay cautious about headcount.
job_market.new_grad_reality: A genuinely tough market for a foreign new grad: roughly two-thirds of UK enterprises are scaling back entry-level hiring as AI absorbs junior tasks, and junior salaries (about £28-40k in London) often don't clear the Skilled Worker visa's sponsorship salary threshold (now above £41,700) in the first place - so foreign new grads compete for a shrinking pool of roles that also happen to meet a salary bar most junior postings don't reach.

language.official: English (Welsh also has co-official status in Wales specifically)
language.pr_citizenship_language_req: Indefinite Leave to Remain (settlement) currently requires 5 years' continuous lawful residence, English at B1, and a pass on the Life in the UK test - but the UK government has confirmed plans to extend this qualifying period from 5 to 10 years, expected around Autumn 2026 (transitional rules for people already mid-residence were unclear in research - verify current Home Office guidance). The English requirement is also set to rise from B1 to B2 from 26 March 2027. Citizenship can follow 12 months after ILR, reusing the English/Life in the UK test plus a 'good character' test.

records.reality_paragraph: Life as a skilled migrant in London is genuinely good professionally, but it sits on top of a housing market close to breaking point. Average Greater London rent hit about £2,280/month in March 2026, now eating roughly 42% of the average renter's income, and fewer than 2% of listed rentals nationwide are affordable to lower earners - most people who move here describe underestimating this before they arrive. Integration on the language and culture front is easy - everything from banking to job interviews runs in English - but the visa system is a long-term source of stress: the government has confirmed the settlement (ILR) qualifying period is moving from 5 to 10 years, resetting the timeline anyone was planning around. London has by far the largest Iranian community of the English-speaking countries here: around 87,700 Persian/Farsi speakers across England & Wales (2021 Census), historically centered around Kensington/West London and now spreading into Barnet, Ealing, Harrow and Brent, with real infrastructure to match. Discrimination isn't universal, but it isn't invented either: reported anti-Muslim and religiously-motivated hate crime has risen sharply since 2024, and that climate affects how Iranians are sometimes perceived regardless of actual religious practice. The most common regret is underestimating how much of your salary rent will eat before you find your footing outside Zone 1-2; the most common thing people say they'd do again is choose London specifically, for the job density and the sheer number of other people who've made the same move.

records.name: Ireland

skilled_routes.name: Critical Skills Employment Permit (CSEP)
skilled_routes.summary: For ICT professionals with a 2-year job offer; no labour market test, immediate family reunification, and after the 2-year permit holders move to Stamp 4 (work without permit). Fee EUR 1,000; apply >=12 weeks before start.
skilled_routes.threshold_note: EUR 40,904 minimum for degree-holders on the Critical Skills list (EUR 36,848 = ~USD 42,400 if qualification obtained within past 12 months; EUR 68,911 for off-list occupations) - verified Aug 2026

study_pathway.note: Non-EU master's tuition typically EUR 12k-25k (est. EUR 16k). Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G): 12 months for level-8 (bachelor) and up to 24 months for level-9+ (master's/PhD) graduates - standing policy; primary pages were unreachable this session, treat as stable but re-verify.

iran_friction.notes: The Irish Times (Apr 2026) reported 'inhumane' family-reunification visa delays for critical-skills workers, with Iranians among those affected. Iranian applicants face months-long study/work entry-visa processing and a small consular footprint (applications handled via third countries/Ankara or Abu Dhabi at times). The permit system itself is nationality-neutral.

dual_citizenship.note: Dual citizenship fully permitted; no renunciation issue for Iranians.

tax.summary: Income tax 20/40% with credits, USC surcharge and 4.2% PRSI; moderate at mid salaries, steep above EUR 44k.
tax.net_note: EUR 55,000 mid-level dev salary; 2025-26 rates (income tax minus EUR 4,000 credits, USC, PRSI 4.2%), own computation (net ~EUR 42,300)
tax.expat_scheme: SARP: 30% income-tax relief on employment income over EUR 100k for qualifying relocated employees (min salary EUR 125k), through 2030

indices.freedom_note: Ireland is rated 'Free' by Freedom House with one of the highest scores globally (98/100) and ranks 14th in Europe for LGBTQ+ rights and law per the ILGA-Europe 2026 Rainbow Map (marriage equality since the 2015 referendum), though a 2026 Trans Rights Index flagged real gaps in trans healthcare access, and Freedom House notes 'some societal discrimination' against Irish Travellers and newly arrived immigrants/asylum seekers.

job_market.summary: Ireland's tech market in 2026 remains resilient and competitive, anchored by Dublin's dense cluster of US tech multinationals alongside secondary hubs in Cork, Galway and Limerick, plus domestic growth in fintech, medtech and AI-powered SaaS. Demand keeps outpacing supply for experienced engineers - AI/ML, cloud, cybersecurity and data roles especially - though hybrid/remote work now means Dublin employers compete directly with Cork, Berlin and Lisbon-based teams for the same developers.
job_market.new_grad_reality: Hard for a non-EU/EEA new grad without an Irish degree: the Critical Skills Employment Permit needs a job offer clearing a salary threshold (~€40,904) that many genuine entry-level roles don't reach, and Dublin's big multinationals mostly sponsor experienced hires, not first jobs. Without an Irish qualification or graduate-route status, the honest picture is a narrow path in.

language.official: Irish (constitutional first official language, Article 8), though English is the de facto majority/working language of government, business and daily life - Irish is not needed for work or citizenship
language.pr_citizenship_language_req: Ireland does NOT require an Irish or English language test for naturalization - one of the few EU countries with no formal language or civics test for citizenship at all. The core requirement is residency: broadly 5 years of 'reckonable residence' (1 year immediately before applying, plus 4 of the previous 8 years), being of 'good character', and a declaration of fidelity to the nation.

records.reality_paragraph: Ireland offers a genuinely warm, English-speaking entry point into Europe with a tech job market still hungry for talent - InterNations' 2025/2026 Expat Insider survey rates Ireland as Europe's best country for working abroad. That collides head-on with what may be the worst housing shortage in Europe right now: Dublin had roughly 1,800-2,300 total rental properties listed across the entire market in early 2026 - the lowest since records began in 2006 - with a typical two-bed apartment averaging about €2,600/month, and housing economists expect the shortage to persist for another decade or more. Integration itself is comparatively easy since naturalization requires no language or civics test at all, unusual even within the EU. The Iranian community, though, is small - informal secondary-source estimates put it around 2,000-3,000 people nationally, mostly students (official CSO figures broken out specifically for Iran were not found and should be verified directly if precision matters), centered on Dublin with small Nowruz and Shab-e Yalda gatherings rather than the dense infrastructure London or Hamburg offer. Discrimination against Iranians specifically isn't documented as a distinct pattern, though Freedom House notes real societal friction nationally around immigration and asylum-seeker accommodation. The most common regret is underestimating how brutal the rental search itself would be; the most common thing people love is how quickly the basics feel workable - English everywhere, genuine tech demand, and a widely-echoed impression of an easier 'settling in' than continental Europe typically offers.

records.name: Germany

skilled_routes.name: EU Blue Card
skilled_routes.summary: For university graduates (or IT specialists with 3+ years experience, no degree needed) with a German job offer. PR after 27 months (21 with B1 German); language not required at entry.
skilled_routes.threshold_note: EUR 50,700 standard / EUR 45,934.20 (~USD 52,900) for IT & bottleneck occupations and graduates within 3 years (45.3% of 2026 pension assessment ceiling)

skilled_routes.name: Opportunity Card (Chancenkarte)
skilled_routes.summary: Points-based 1-year job-search residence (education, experience, language, age); requires blocked-account funds, allows 20h/week trial work. Converts to work permit/Blue Card on hire.
skilled_routes.threshold_note: No salary threshold; points + ~EUR 13k blocked account

study_pathway.note: Public universities are tuition-free for most master's programs (semester fee EUR 150-400); exception: Baden-Wuerttemberg charges non-EU students EUR 1,500/semester (~USD 3,500/yr). 18-month job-seeking residence permit after graduation.

iran_friction.notes: The German Embassy Tehran has chronic appointment backlogs for national (work/study) visas - often a year or more for some categories. In late 2025 it paused and then resumed Schengen operations while Germany accused Iran of withholding diplomat visas, 'crippling embassy operations'; Iran International reported Iranians stranded and separated from families by German visa delays (Nov 2025). The 2026 regional conflict adds travel and document-legalization disruption. Blue Card applicants get some priority but long waits remain standard for Iranians.

dual_citizenship.note: Multiple nationality allowed without restriction since 27 Jun 2024, so Iran's renunciation bar is irrelevant. Note: the 3-year fast-track naturalization was abolished in Oct 2025; standard is 5 years.

tax.summary: Progressive income tax (14-45%) plus heavy employee social contributions (~21%: pension, health, care, unemployment); overall one of the highest wedges in the OECD.
tax.net_note: EUR 60,000 mid-level dev salary, tax class I; 2026 tariff + social contributions, own computation cross-checked against BMF/SteuerGo-style calculators (net ~EUR 37,100)

indices.freedom_note: Germany is legally progressive on paper - marriage equality since 2017, a Self-Determination Act since November 2024 letting trans/non-binary/intersex people change legal name and gender by simple declaration - but the political climate has cooled sharply, with the far-right AfD (20.8% in the 2025 federal election, formally designated a 'right-wing extremist' entity by German domestic intelligence in May 2025) coinciding with a documented 40% jump in politically-motivated hate crimes in 2024, including sharp rises in anti-Muslim and anti-LGBTQ+ incidents.

job_market.summary: Germany's IT sector is a bright spot inside a stagnant wider economy (GDP growth ~1.2% in 2026): over 137,000 IT positions reportedly sit unfilled, making it one of the more accessible major economies for qualified tech workers. Hiring is concentrated in Berlin (fintech, B2B SaaS), Munich (enterprise/automotive software, highest ML/AI salaries), and secondary hubs Hamburg and Frankfurt. Layoffs have been less of a defining story here than in UK/US tech - the binding constraint is unfilled vacancies rather than headcount cuts.
job_market.new_grad_reality: On paper favorable - IT is an official shortage occupation, lowering the EU Blue Card salary threshold (~€45,934, further reduced for recent grads) - but the practical filter is German-language ability: outside a handful of Berlin-style English-first startups, most employers, especially in Munich or traditional enterprise, expect at least conversational German, narrowing the realistic playing field well below the headline vacancy numbers.

language.pr_citizenship_language_req: Two distinct tracks. (1) Citizenship/naturalization: the June 2024 reform cut the standard residency requirement from 8 to 5 years and now permits full dual citizenship, but requires German at B1; the 3-year 'fast-track' route (which had required C1 German) was abolished effective 30 October 2025, so 5 years plus B1 is now the only naturalization path. A still-active 1929 Germany-Iran treaty requires German authorities to seek Iranian government approval before naturalizing Iranian nationals - a real, usually procedural, extra step (most Iranian-Germans end up holding both nationalities in practice, since Iran rarely formally releases citizens). (2) Permanent settlement (Niederlassungserlaubnis) is separate: EU Blue Card holders can qualify after just 21 months with B1 German, or 27 months with only basic A1, versus 33 months for other Blue Card cases or 4 years for general skilled workers - reaching this quickly does not shortcut the 5-year/B1 citizenship clock.

records.reality_paragraph: Germany is the classic 'the work is fine, the paperwork will break you' migration story. InterNations' Expat Insider survey ranked Germany 30th of 31 countries in both 2025 and 2026 - second-to-last overall - specifically because of bureaucracy (65% of expats rate it negatively), slow digitization, and a cash-heavy admin culture, even though 60% of respondents still say they're personally happy living there. Cost of living is genuinely more affordable than London or Dublin on average, but city rents are still up about 44% versus 2016, and finding housing in Berlin or Munich is its own real struggle. Integration is the theme that comes up in almost every serious account: even in English-speaking tech jobs - genuinely common in Berlin, less so in Munich or outside the startup bubble - daily life outside the office (the Bürgeramt, the tax office, apartment contracts) runs in German and is frequently described as opaque even by people who speak German well. Germany has by a wide margin the largest and most historically rooted Iranian community of the English/native-adjacent comparison set here: an estimated 319,000 people of Iranian background nationally (2024 Destatis estimate; a narrower count of 114,125 Iranian citizens specifically was recorded in 2021), concentrated in Berlin, Munich, Hamburg (which alone has at least 20,000 Iranians and trade ties to Iran going back over a century), Frankfurt and Heidelberg. Discrimination is a documented pattern here, not just an impression: hate crime statistics rose sharply through 2024-2025 alongside the AfD's rise, and academic research on second-generation Iranian-Germans describes persistent feelings of marginalization despite high education and language fluency. The most common regret is underestimating how isolating the language-and-bureaucracy barrier feels even when your job runs entirely in English; what people say they'd do again is the quality-of-life basics - job security, healthcare, vacation time, public transit - plus, for Iranians specifically, landing in a community large enough to feel like an actual community.
flags: German bureaucracy/paperwork culture is a well-documented, repeated shock - Germany ranked 2nd-to-last of 31 countries in InterNations Expat Insider, two years running
English-friendly tech jobs are real but concentrated in Berlin - do not assume this reflects Munich or the national market
AfD's rise and a documented 40% jump in 2024 politically-motivated hate crimes are a real, current part of the climate
3-year fast-track citizenship route was abolished October 2025 - 5 years plus B1 German is now the only naturalization path
A 1929 Germany-Iran treaty requires Iranian-government approval before naturalizing Iranian nationals
Don't conflate Niederlassungserlaubnis (settlement, possible in ~21 months with B1) with citizenship (5-year minimum, separate process)

records.name: Netherlands

skilled_routes.name: Highly Skilled Migrant (kennismigrant)
skilled_routes.summary: Employer must be an IND-recognized sponsor; very fast (2-4 weeks). Age-banded salary criteria; a reduced criterion applies within 3 years of graduation/orientation year.
skilled_routes.threshold_note: 2026 gross/month excl. holiday allowance: EUR 5,942 (30+) = ~USD 82,100/yr; EUR 4,357 (<30) = ~USD 60,200/yr; EUR 3,122 reduced criterion after Dutch study = ~USD 43,100/yr (IND official)

skilled_routes.name: EU Blue Card (NL)
skilled_routes.summary: Alternative to HSM with EU-wide mobility perks; recognized sponsorship not strictly required.
skilled_routes.threshold_note: EUR 5,942/month 2026; reduced EUR 4,754 (~USD 65,700/yr) for graduates within 3 years

study_pathway.note: Non-EU master's institutional tuition typically EUR 16k-22k (est. EUR 19k). Orientation year (zoekjaar hoogopgeleiden): 12 months unrestricted work; usable within 3 years of graduation and unlocks the reduced HSM salary criterion.

iran_friction.notes: Dutch knowledge-security screening targets sensitive tech fields and universities have rejected hundreds of 'risky' international researchers (NL Times 2025); Iranian students were historically constrained by sanctions-era rules. MVV collection in Tehran and sanctions banking add delays, and tuition/maintenance transfers from Iran are hard. The HSM route itself is fast and nationality-neutral via recognized sponsors.

dual_citizenship.note: Naturalization normally requires renouncing, BUT a statutory exception applies when the origin country's law does not allow renunciation - Iranians are treated as unable to renounce in practice, so they effectively keep Iranian citizenship (exception documented in Dutch nationality law).

tax.summary: Box-1 progressive tax (~35.7%/37.6%/49.5% in 2026) with substantial general and labour tax credits; no separate employee social premiums beyond box 1.
tax.net_note: EUR 60,000 mid-level dev salary; 2026 box-1 rates and credits, own computation (net ~EUR 43,700), excl. 30% ruling
tax.expat_scheme: 30% ruling: ~30% of salary tax-free for up to 5 years for recruited expats (27% from 2027 for new grants; salary norm applies) - big boost to net pay

indices.freedom_note: The Netherlands ranks among the world's freest press environments (2nd of 180 in the 2026 RSF World Press Freedom Index) and has strong legal LGBTQ+ protections - reinforced by a 2026 conversion-therapy ban and the country's first openly gay prime minister (Rob Jetten) taking office in February 2026 - but reported LGBTQ+ discrimination and hate incidents have been rising per a 2026 police/anti-discrimination agency report, and the political climate has shifted toward a more conservative, immigration-skeptical coalition.

job_market.summary: Dutch tech hiring in 2026 is bifurcated: layoffs have hit generalist and platform-ops roles (ASML cut ~1,700 jobs in January 2026 despite strong AI-driven demand; Amsterdam also saw cuts at Just Eat Takeaway, Bird, and TomTom), while demand for MLOps, LLM engineering, cloud, and cybersecurity specialists keeps rising, with ICT vacancies still numbering roughly 23,000. Amsterdam (Booking.com, Adyen, Databricks, the wider scaleup ecosystem) and Brainport Eindhoven (ASML and its supply chain) are the two main hubs.
job_market.new_grad_reality: Realistically moderate-to-hard: junior roles rarely come with direct visa sponsorship, but the one-year 'orientation year' (zoekjaar) visa for recent graduates of a Dutch university (or a short list of top-ranked foreign universities) lets you job-hunt without a sponsor and then qualify for a reduced Highly Skilled Migrant salary threshold (~€3,122/month) - without that route, landing a first sponsored dev job as a new grad is a tough ask.

language.pr_citizenship_language_req: Civic integration (inburgering) is mandatory for both permanent residence and naturalisation. As of mid-2026 the standard requirement remains Dutch level A2 (via the integration-exam route, after 5 years of legal residence); there has been recurring political discussion about raising this to B1, and a rumored mid-2026 change did not materialize - this is genuinely in flux and should be re-verified against IND/government.nl before relying on it.

records.reality_paragraph: For a skilled migrant on a Highly Skilled Migrant or EU Blue Card visa, day-to-day life in the Netherlands is genuinely comfortable: the tech job itself is very likely to run in English, bureaucracy is largely digitized, and infrastructure, healthcare, and work-life balance are strong by any standard. The catch is housing - Amsterdam's private rental market has a structural regional shortage of roughly 45,000-47,000 homes, a one-bedroom in the free sector averages around €2,200/month, and decent listings often disappear within 24-48 hours, so budget serious time and money for the search (Eindhoven and Rotterdam are somewhat easier). The Iranian community here is the most established of the Continental European countries in this comparison - tens of thousands of people, with roots going back to the 1979 revolution and a visible, multi-generational presence of student associations and cultural organizations in Amsterdam, Rotterdam, The Hague, and especially Delft; this is an impression from community reporting rather than a rigorous survey, but the consistent sense is of an accessible network. Integration still takes real effort: civic integration with a Dutch exam is mandatory for permanent residence and citizenship, and while your job and early daily life can run almost entirely in English, many people report hitting a ceiling in mid-level bureaucracy, healthcare navigation, and workplace social life if they never move past English. Discrimination isn't absent - LGBTQ+ hate-incident reports have risen recently even as legal protections stay strong - but the country's anti-discrimination institutions remain among the strongest in Europe. A commonly reported regret is underestimating the housing search and the isolation of the first year before language and local friendships catch up; a commonly cited thing people love is the sheer predictability of the place - functioning trains, bike infrastructure, and a tech scene where you can build a real career without ever mastering Dutch.
flags: Severe Amsterdam housing shortage - regional deficit of ~45,000-47,000 homes; 1-bed private rentals average ~€2,200/month and can vanish within 24-48 hours of listing
Entry-level tech roles rarely come with direct visa sponsorship - the 'orientation year' route matters much more than usual for new grads
30% expat tax ruling drops to 27% for rulings granted from 1 January 2027 onward
A2 Dutch is required for PR/citizenship today, but political pressure to raise it to B1 is ongoing - verify current status
Reported LGBTQ+ discrimination/hate incidents rising despite strong legal protections

records.name: Italy

skilled_routes.name: EU Blue Card (Italy)
skilled_routes.summary: Post-2023 reform: open to graduates, IT specialists with 3 years' experience, and quota-exempt (outside decreto flussi). Salary must meet the applicable national collective agreement (CCNL) level.
skilled_routes.threshold_note: No fixed national euro threshold published for 2026; salary must not be below the relevant CCNL rate (in practice roughly EUR 25k-35k). Not verified against an official 2026 figure this session.

skilled_routes.name: Decreto Flussi work visa
skilled_routes.summary: Annual quota system (500k visas planned 2026-28) with 'click day' applications; mostly non-graduate roles, slow and unpredictable - Blue Card is the realistic dev route.
skilled_routes.threshold_note: Quota-based; no skill salary threshold

study_pathway.note: Public-university fees are income-scaled, typically EUR 900-4,000/yr for non-EU students (est. EUR 2,500); many scholarships (DSU) even cover living costs. Graduates can convert to a 12-month 'attesa occupazione' (job-seeking) permit.

iran_friction.notes: Main frictions are consular: scarce appointment slots at the Italian Embassy Tehran for study (Universitaly pre-enrolment) and work visas, plus document legalization queues. Italy actively recruits international students (incl. many Iranians) and renewed that commitment in Nov 2025; the 2026 regional conflict adds travel/banking disruption. No documented Iran-specific refusal pattern beyond consular capacity.

dual_citizenship.note: Dual citizenship permitted; no renunciation issue. Note: 10-year residence requirement (a June 2025 referendum to cut it to 5 failed on turnout), plus ~2-3 years' application processing in practice.

tax.summary: IRPEF 23-43% plus ~9.2% employee INPS contributions and regional/municipal surtaxes.
tax.net_note: EUR 45,000 mid-level dev salary; 2025-26 IRPEF + INPS 9.19% + ~2% local surtaxes, own computation (net ~EUR 29,500)
tax.expat_scheme: Lavoratori impatriati: 50% of employment income exempt for 5 years (cap EUR 600k, degree + residency conditions)

indices.freedom_note: Italy's press freedom has been declining (56th of 180 in the 2026 RSF Index, down from 49th in 2025, amid a 'gag law' restricting court reporting and political pressure on public broadcaster RAI), and LGBTQ+ people have meaningfully weaker legal protections than in the Netherlands or Spain - civil unions but no marriage equality, conversion therapy not banned, and a governing coalition actively pursuing rollbacks including limits on registering both parents in same-sex couples.

job_market.summary: Italy's IT job market grew an estimated 18% in 2026 (roughly 12,000 new positions), heavily concentrated in Milan (about 55% of openings, plus an 11% salary premium over the national average), with Rome (~20%, largely public-sector IT/cybersecurity) and Turin (~8%, automotive/mobility tech around Stellantis) well behind. Demand is strongest for full-stack, cloud, AI, and cybersecurity roles, with typical developer salaries around €35,000-65,000, but the market outside Milan and a handful of multinational offices remains considerably more local and Italian-language-driven.
job_market.new_grad_reality: Hard: Italy has no early-career visa shortcut, entry-level salaries (roughly €28,000-35,000) sit close to typical sponsorship thresholds, non-EU work permits run through the capped annual decreto flussi quota system (the EU Blue Card sits outside the quota but requires a qualifying job offer), and most employers outside a handful of Milan multinationals and internationally-facing startups expect at least functional Italian even for technical roles.

language.pr_citizenship_language_req: Citizenship by residency requires 10 years of continuous legal residence - one of the longest qualifying periods in the EU - plus a certified B1 Italian language level (required since 2018), proof of sufficient annual income (minimum roughly €8,263 for a single applicant), and a clean criminal record in both Italy and the home country.

records.reality_paragraph: Life for a skilled migrant in Italy involves a real trade-off: the lifestyle, food, and climate are genuinely valued by expats and frequently cited as the reason people stay despite a tougher bureaucratic and economic environment than Northern Europe. Milan is the only city where the tech job market resembles what a CS grad might expect from Northern Europe or the US, and even there, English gets you through the office but not through daily life - renting an apartment, dealing with the questura for your permesso di soggiorno, opening a bank account, or seeing a doctor outside a private international clinic will require functional Italian fairly quickly. Housing adds real pressure: rental vacancy in Milan and Rome sits at roughly 1-3%, among the tightest in Western Europe, rents rose nationally by about 6.6% over the past year, and a typical city-center one-bedroom in Milan can absorb around 72% of an average net Italian salary (about 65% in Rome). The Iranian community is small and comparatively new - official residency figures put it at roughly 20,000-24,000 people nationally (sources vary by year and measure), having reportedly doubled since 2019, concentrated in Rome and Milan and skewing toward students, about half of them women - a much thinner, newer network than the Netherlands' community. Italy has no strong points-based tech visa - non-EU nationals go through either the EU Blue Card or the capped decreto flussi quota system - and the path to citizenship by residency is 10 years plus a B1 Italian certificate. Discrimination against migrants generally isn't the top-cited concern in available sources, but the current government's rhetoric and rollback of same-sex-parent recognition are worth knowing about, and press freedom has been declining amid gag-law and public-broadcaster concerns. The most common regret is underestimating how much the language barrier and slow bureaucracy affect daily life even when the job itself is in English; the most consistently cited thing people love is the quality of life once the administrative hurdles are cleared.

Low share of English-only tech jobs outside Milan multinationals and international-facing startups
10-year residency requirement for citizenship (one of the longest in the EU) plus a B1 Italian certificate
Milan/Rome rental vacancy near 1-3%; Milan center rent can absorb ~72% of an average net salary
Press freedom declining - dropped from 49th to 56th of 180 (RSF, 2025 to 2026)
Weaker LGBTQ+ legal protections than NL/ES - civil unions only, no marriage equality, conversion therapy not banned
Small, recent Iranian community (~20,000-24,000 nationally), concentrated in Rome/Milan, largely students

records.name: Spain

skilled_routes.name: EU Blue Card / Highly Qualified Professional (Ley 14/2013)
skilled_routes.summary: Fast-track UGE processing (~20 working days) for graduate-level hires; Blue Card thresholds were reset by Order PJC/44/2026.
skilled_routes.threshold_note: EUR 39,269.92/yr (1.4x average gross income, 2026); reduced EUR 31,415.94 = ~USD 36,200 for shortage-list roles and graduates within 3 years (official, Order PJC/44/2026)

skilled_routes.name: Digital Nomad Visa (teletrabajo)
skilled_routes.summary: Remote-work residence for employees/freelancers of foreign companies; popular fallback for devs (income requirement ~200% SMI, ~EUR 2,800/mo).
skilled_routes.threshold_note: ~200% of minimum wage; verify current SMI

study_pathway.note: Public master's fees are per-credit and region-dependent; non-EU students typically EUR 1.5k-8k/yr (est. EUR 4.5k). Graduates can take a 12-month job-search/entrepreneurship stay or (since the 2025 immigration regulation) switch directly to work status; students may work up to 30h/week.

iran_friction.notes: Frictions are mostly consular and administrative: limited appointment capacity for legalizations/visas in Tehran, sanctions banking for transferring funds, and slow civil-registry steps later on. Evidence of an Iran-specific refusal pattern is thinner than for AU/CA/DE - treat level as an informed estimate. The big structural bar is citizenship: 10 years plus renunciation formalities.

dual_citizenship.note: Naturalizers from non-Ibero-American countries must formally declare renunciation of their prior nationality before the Civil Registry. Spain does not verify effective loss under foreign law and Iran does not recognize renunciation, so Iranians de facto retain Iranian nationality - but formally Spain treats it as renounced and using it can theoretically prejudice Spanish nationality.

tax.summary: Progressive IRPF (19-47% combined state+regional) plus ~6.5% employee social security.
tax.net_note: EUR 45,000 mid-level dev salary; 2025-26 IRPF (state+typical regional scale) + 6.48% SS, own computation (net ~EUR 32,600)
tax.expat_scheme: Beckham law: opt-in 24% flat tax on employment income up to EUR 600k for 6 years for new residents

indices.freedom_note: Spain combines strong, comprehensive legal LGBTQ+ protections (full marriage equality, joint adoption rights, banned conversion therapy) and a press freedom ranking that remains solidly good (29th of 180 in the 2026 RSF Index, though down from 23rd in 2025) with a more polarized political climate marked by the rise of the far-right Vox party and increased harassment of journalists.

job_market.summary: Spain's tech hiring is concentrated in Madrid (~47% of software engineering openings) and Barcelona (~27%), with Valencia, Malaga, and Bilbao emerging as smaller hubs; AI/ML, cloud, and cybersecurity roles are growing fastest, and the government's 'Digital Spain 2026' initiative is actively pushing international recruitment because digital specialists remain a smaller share of the workforce (3.2%) than the EU average (3.9%). Employers report raising pay significantly to compete for scarce senior talent, though entry-level competition remains stiff.
job_market.new_grad_reality: Also hard for a true first job with zero experience, though structurally a bit more favorable than Italy - Spain has no points-based visa either, but is actively simplifying its Highly Qualified Professional visa and EU Blue Card route, and Barcelona's startup/multinational scene and Madrid's international base offer the best odds of an English-language hiring process, provided you can clear the initial bar without local experience or a strong network.

language.official: Spanish (Castilian); Catalan, Basque, and Galician are co-official regional languages in their respective autonomous communities but are not required for national residency or citizenship processes
language.pr_citizenship_language_req: Citizenship by residency requires 10 years of continuous legal residence for Iranian nationals - the reduced 2-year route applies only to Ibero-American countries, the Philippines, Andorra, Equatorial Guinea, Portugal, and people of Sephardic origin, not Iran - plus passing the DELE A2 Spanish language exam (~€130) and the CCSE Spanish culture/constitution test (~€85). Real-world processing time reportedly ranges from about 3 to 24 months depending on the regional civil registry's backlog.

records.reality_paragraph: Spain offers something the Netherlands and Italy don't quite match for many skilled migrants: a genuinely well-liked lifestyle - climate, food, and a slower pace of life are consistently cited by expats as the reason they stay, though that's a subjective, self-reported signal rather than a hard metric. The tech job market is real and growing - Madrid and Barcelona together account for roughly three-quarters of software engineering openings, Barcelona in particular has a genuinely English-friendly startup and multinational scene (the 22@ district), and 'Digital Spain 2026' is actively trying to ease international hiring because digital specialists are a documented gap in the workforce. That said, outside the Madrid/Barcelona international bubble, Spanish is expected for most roles, and daily bureaucracy - NIE/TIE paperwork, banking, healthcare registration - runs in Spanish regardless of what language your job is in. Housing is under real pressure in both major cities as part of a broader national debate over rent and tourism-driven housing costs, though current, precisely-citable figures were not confidently located in this research pass - treat this as a real budgeting risk rather than a footnote. The Iranian community is the smallest of the Continental European countries covered here - official statistics put it at somewhere between roughly 5,000 and 10,000 people depending on the year and whether measured by nationality or birthplace, concentrated in Madrid (about a third), Barcelona, and Malaga, with roots tracing to the 1979 revolution - a noticeably smaller, less institutionally visible community than the Netherlands'. Spain has no points-based tech visa either - it relies on the employer-sponsored Highly Qualified Professional visa and EU Blue Card - and citizenship by residency takes 10 years for Iranian nationals, plus the DELE A2 exam and the CCSE test. A commonly reported regret is underestimating the Spanish-language requirement for anything outside the international tech bubble; the most consistently cited thing people love is quality of life - outdoor culture, food, and climate - which shows up repeatedly in independent expat-satisfaction surveys.

10-year residency requirement for citizenship - the 2-year fast track does not apply to Iranian nationals
Madrid/Barcelona rent and housing pressure is significant - specific current figures were not independently verified in this research pass

records.name: Sweden

skilled_routes.name: Work permit (arbetstillstand)
skilled_routes.summary: Employer-offer permit; advertised job + collective-agreement-level terms. From 1 Jun 2026 the salary floor is 90% of the Swedish median wage, and the Migration Agency can refuse over employer deficiencies. Certified employers get ~2-week processing.
skilled_routes.threshold_note: SEK 34,470/month (90% of SCB median, updated 16 Jun 2026) = ~SEK 413,640/yr; 27 exempt occupations at 75%; transitional 80% rule for pre-Jun-2026 permit holders until 1 Dec 2026

skilled_routes.name: EU Blue Card (SE)
skilled_routes.summary: Now grantable up to 4 years; higher salary bar than the ordinary permit but EU mobility benefits.
skilled_routes.threshold_note: SEK 52,000/month (unchanged 2026) = ~SEK 624,000/yr

study_pathway.note: Non-EU master's tuition typically SEK 120k-145k/yr (est. SEK 140k); generous university scholarships exist. After graduation: 12-month residence permit to seek work or start a business.

iran_friction.notes: SAPO security vetting has blocked or revoked permits and citizenship for a number of Iranian researchers/engineers in dual-use fields - covered as 'Sweden is ruining people's careers' (The Local, 2025) and 'Sweden's security service has gone a little crazy' (Meduza, 2025). Ordinary dev roles usually clear, and Sweden hosts a very large Iranian diaspora. From Jun 2026, stricter salary, self-sufficiency and (from Aug 2026) civics-test requirements raise general hurdles including for pending citizenship files, which are re-assessed under the new 8-year rule.

dual_citizenship.note: Dual citizenship permitted since 2001; no renunciation issue. Citizenship reform (in force 6 Jun 2026): 8 years' residence (up from 5), self-sufficiency (income >= 3 income base amounts), civics/language tests phased in from Aug 2026/Oct 2027 - applied even to already-pending applications.

tax.summary: Municipal tax ~32% (plus 20% state tax above ~SEK 640k/yr) softened by earned-income tax credit; no separate employee social fees.
tax.net_note: SEK 45,000/month (540,000/yr) mid-level dev; municipal ~32% with jobbskatteavdrag, below state-tax threshold, own computation (net ~SEK 410,000), Ekonomifakta-style
tax.expat_scheme: Expert tax relief: 25% of remuneration tax-free for up to 7 years for qualifying foreign experts/high earners

indices.freedom_note: Sweden ranks 5th globally on RSF's 2026 World Press Freedom Index and has strong LGBTQ+ legal protections (marriage equality since 2009), but the national-conservative Sweden Democrats are now the second-largest party in the Riksdag and immigration policy has shifted markedly rightward heading into the 13 September 2026 general election.

job_market.summary: Sweden's 2026 tech market is selective rather than booming: national unemployment sits around 8%, but software developers remain consistently in demand, IT salaries have risen sharply, and AI/cloud skills are especially sought after per TechSverige's January 2026 labour-market analysis. Stockholm (fintech/gaming/startups - the Spotify/Klarna/King/Mojang heritage), Gothenburg (automotive/industrial tech) and Malmo are the main hubs, but hiring isn't uniformly hot: gaming has seen real layoffs (DICE Stockholm cut roughly 640 to 420 staff 2022-24, Paradox Interactive cut 50+) and startup funding is down about 47% from its 2021 peak.
job_market.new_grad_reality: Realistically hard but not impossible: many junior postings still list conversational Swedish as a plus or requirement outside the most international scale-ups, and from 1 June 2026 a new non-EU work-permit salary floor (90% of the Swedish median, roughly SEK 33,390/month) may sit above some genuinely entry-level offers, so sponsorship terms are worth checking before counting on a specific job.

language.pr_citizenship_language_req: Verified current as of 6 June 2026 (new law, no transitional protection for pending cases): the habitual residence requirement rose from 5 to 8 years (2 years for Nordic citizens, 7 for refugees/spouses); a new self-sufficiency test requires income of at least three income-base-amounts/year (~SEK 250,200/year) sustained for 3 consecutive years, with welfare receipt capped at 6 months in that window; and knowledge of Swedish and Swedish society is now mandatory for applicants aged 16-66, shown via school grades/SFI course D/komvux, or a citizenship test (medborgarskapsprovet) if no such evidence exists. The society-knowledge test began a Stockholm-only pilot on 15 August 2026; a dedicated Swedish-language test is legislated but not yet active, expected 1 October 2027 at the earliest. Dual citizenship remains allowed (since 2001).

records.reality_paragraph: Sweden is the one Nordic country where a skilled Iranian migrant can plug into a genuinely large, multi-generational community rather than starting from zero: Statistics Sweden counted 87,292 Iran-born residents in 2025 (plus tens of thousands more Sweden-born to Iranian parents), and Iranian-Swedes have reached the Riksdag (about a dozen MPs after the 2022 election) and cabinet posts. Professionally, Stockholm's startup/gaming/fintech scene is genuinely English-friendly and meritocratic, but housing is a real shock: Stockholm's public rental system runs on queue time, not income, and it became 'essentially impossible' during the 2010s to get a lease with under five years in the queue, with central addresses often taking far longer - most newcomers end up in the pricier private sublet or ownership market instead. Income tax is high (Sweden is routinely near the top of OECD tax-burden rankings). Socially, the pattern described in InterNations' annual Expat Insider survey - an impression, but a very consistently repeated one for the Nordic region - is that Sweden is professionally welcoming and personally slow: colleagues are warm, but close Swedish friendships can take years to form. There's no verifiable pattern of discrimination specific to Iranian migrants, but the political backdrop has shifted: citizenship rules tightened sharply on 6 June 2026 and the Sweden Democrats' rise has pulled mainstream migration rhetoric rightward over the past decade. What people commonly regret is underestimating the housing queue and the multi-year timeline to real social integration; what they commonly love is the flat workplace hierarchy, real work-life balance and parental leave, and - for Iranians specifically - that Stockholm's community is large enough to actually build a life within.

Citizenship residency requirement just rose from 5 to 8 years (6 June 2026), plus new income/self-sufficiency test and mandatory civics test
Swedish-language citizenship test still to come (~Oct 2027 earliest)

records.name: Denmark

skilled_routes.name: Pay Limit Scheme
skilled_routes.summary: Any job qualifies if pay is high enough and matches Danish standards; salary must be paid into a Danish bank account. Fast (1 month normal). Supplementary lower-threshold track exists for certified companies.
skilled_routes.threshold_note: DKK 552,000/yr minimum for 2026 (official nyidanmark.dk; indexed annually); supplementary scheme has a lower bar (~DKK 415k+, employer-certified)

skilled_routes.name: Positive List for Higher Education
skilled_routes.summary: Shortage-occupation route (software developers regularly listed) without the Pay Limit salary floor - pay must still match Danish standards.
skilled_routes.threshold_note: No fixed threshold; collective-agreement-level pay required

study_pathway.note: Non-EU tuition typically DKK 75k-120k/yr (est. DKK 100k). Graduates of state-approved Danish programs automatically get a 3-year job-seeking period with full work rights (6 months for some non-state-approved programs; none for those applied for after 2 May 2025).

iran_friction.notes: No documented Iran-specific refusal pattern; standard security screening applies. Practical frictions: opening the mandatory Danish bank account within 180 days, sanctions-related transfer/document issues from Iran, and 2026 conflict travel disruption. Denmark's high salary floor is the real gate, not nationality.

dual_citizenship.note: Dual citizenship permitted since Sept 2015; no renunciation issue. Citizenship itself is slow: 9 years' residence (last 2 as permanent resident), PR normally 8 years (4 on fast-track).

tax.summary: 8% AM-bidrag plus bottom/municipal taxes (~37% combined at mid incomes, top tax above ~DKK 640k); no other employee social contributions.
tax.net_note: DKK 550,000 mid-level dev salary; AM-bidrag + bottom/municipal tax with employment deduction, own computation (net ~DKK 352,000), Skat.dk-style
tax.expat_scheme: Researcher/key-employee scheme: flat 27% + AM-bidrag (~32.8% total) for up to 7 years (2026 min salary ~DKK 78,000/month)

indices.freedom_note: Denmark ranks 4th globally on RSF's 2026 World Press Freedom Index and has strong LGBTQ+ protections (the world's first registered-partnership law in 1989, marriage equality since 2012), but successive governments - including the governing Social Democrats - have pursued a deliberately restrictive immigration and integration policy for over a decade, which shapes political rhetoric more than any documented pattern of day-to-day treatment of skilled migrants.

job_market.summary: Denmark's tech sector shows a structural shortage rather than a hiring freeze: industry estimates cite a 7,000+ IT-specialist gap and a projected 13,000 STEM graduate shortfall by 2030, with steady demand for software engineers, cloud, data and cybersecurity roles. Copenhagen dominates (roughly 83% of software-developer openings) with Aarhus a distant second hub; no Denmark-specific 2026 tech-layoff wave was found in research, though global layoffs at multinationals with a Danish presence remain a background risk as anywhere.
job_market.new_grad_reality: The structural shortage helps, but Denmark's work-permit salary gates are real: the general Pay Limit Scheme requires a job offer of at least DKK 552,000/year (2026) - above many entry-level salaries - so the more realistic route for a non-EU new grad is Denmark's lower-threshold Positive List for shortage occupations (IT roles are regularly included), which is worth checking against the specific offer in hand.

language.pr_citizenship_language_req: Confirmed via Denmark's official citizen-information site (lifeindenmark.borger.dk), and this is genuinely the strictest regime in the Nordics: 9 years of continuous residence as the general rule (8 for refugees/stateless, 2 for Nordic citizens, 6-8 for spouses of Danish citizens depending on marriage length); a Danish language test at level 3 ('Dansk 3' / Prøve i Dansk 3, widely described in secondary sources as roughly CEFR B2); a citizenship test ('Indfødsretsprøven af 2021'); proof of ordinary full-time employment for at least 3 years and 6 months of the last 4 years; no social-assistance receipt at all in the 2 years before applying (max 4 months total in the preceding 5 years); a clean criminal record; and a signed declaration of allegiance. Uniquely among the Nordics, citizenship is granted only via an individual Act of Parliament, followed by a mandatory municipal ceremony. Denmark has allowed dual citizenship since 2015 (stable and well-established, though not re-verified against a primary source in this research pass).

records.reality_paragraph: Denmark's Iranian community is real but modest: Statistics Denmark counted about 28,491 people of Iranian background (immigrants plus Danish-born descendants combined) as of 2025 - the 10th-largest immigrant-origin group in the country - concentrated in and around Copenhagen, versus roughly 87,000 Iran-born alone in Sweden, so newcomers should expect a much smaller, tighter-knit network rather than a large ready-made community. Copenhagen's tech scene is genuinely strong and operates comfortably in English at the company level, but Denmark pairs that openness with the toughest naturalization bar in the Nordics and work-permit salary floors that can sit above entry-level pay. Income tax is high - Denmark is consistently near the top of OECD tax-burden rankings. Social integration follows the pattern InterNations' Expat Insider survey has reported for years: Denmark is specifically and repeatedly singled out by expats as one of the harder European countries in which to build close local friendships, even when colleagues are warm and professional - a widely cited survey impression, not a universal experience. Danish immigration politics have trended restrictive across governments of multiple parties for over a decade; there is no verifiable pattern of discrimination specific to Iranian migrants beyond that general policy climate. The common regret people report is underestimating the language-plus-employment-history bar for citizenship and the small size of the diaspora network outside Copenhagen; the common draw is Denmark's strong welfare state, Copenhagen's liveability and cycling culture, and a genuinely humane work-life balance.

records.name: Norway

skilled_routes.name: Skilled worker residence permit
skilled_routes.summary: For degree-holders (or certified trades) with a Norwegian job offer; pay must match Norwegian norms - UDI enforces explicit salary floors where no collective agreement applies.
skilled_routes.threshold_note: From 1 Sep 2025: NOK 599,200/yr for master's-level positions, NOK 522,600 (~USD 54,800) for bachelor's-level (UDI via EIG)

skilled_routes.name: Job-seeker permit for graduates/researchers
skilled_routes.summary: 12-month post-completion permit for those who studied/researched in Norway, with work rights while searching (regular foreign job-seeker variant is 6 months, no work).
skilled_routes.threshold_note: No salary threshold; funds requirement

study_pathway.note: Tuition-free era ended autumn 2023 for non-EU/EEA students; fees vary hugely (NOK 150k-580k/yr by program/university; est. NOK 250k). 12-month graduate job-seeker permit with work rights.

iran_friction.notes: Norway has a documented history of export-control screening hitting Iranian students and researchers in technical fields (2014-16 rejection/deportation cases; continued vetting for sensitive subjects incl. some CS/AI specializations). Employment-based skilled-worker visas are generally processed normally, though UDI wait times drew complaints in 2026. Sanctions banking friction applies to funds from Iran.

dual_citizenship.note: Dual citizenship permitted since 1 Jan 2020; no renunciation issue. Citizenship requires ~8 of the last 11 years' residence (B1 Norwegian and self-support conditions apply).

tax.summary: 22% ordinary tax after deductions plus progressive bracket tax and 7.7% national insurance.
tax.net_note: NOK 750,000 mid-level dev salary; 2025-26 rates (ordinary tax with minimum/personal deductions, bracket tax, NI), own computation (net ~NOK 550,000), Skatteetaten-style
tax.expat_scheme: Optional flat 25% PAYE scheme for foreign workers in their first year (income cap ~NOK 700k)

indices.freedom_note: Norway ranks 1st globally on RSF's 2026 World Press Freedom Index and has strong LGBTQ+ legal protections (marriage equality since 2009); anti-immigration politics exist mainly via the Progress Party but are comparatively less dominant in day-to-day national debate than in Sweden or Denmark, though this is a general impression rather than a polling-verified claim.

job_market.summary: Norway's tech sector is smaller than Sweden's or Denmark's but genuinely tight on talent: the Norwegian Computer Society projects a need for 16,000+ additional developers, and NHO's Kompetansebarometer has talent scarcity as the top-cited obstacle to growth for roughly 30% of executives. Oslo is the clear hub (roughly half of all Norwegian IT jobs, strong in fintech/startups), with Bergen (ocean/maritime tech), Trondheim and Stavanger as secondary centres; pay is high in absolute terms, underpinned by Norway's oil-linked public wealth.
job_market.new_grad_reality: Talent scarcity works somewhat in a new grad's favour, and junior developer pay is high in absolute terms (roughly NOK 500,000-900,000/year depending on city, role and source), but Norway is a small market with correspondingly few new-grad-specific openings, so the realistic path is a relevant degree plus a genuine skills match rather than a mass graduate-scheme culture.

language.official: Norwegian (Bokmål/Nynorsk); Sámi has official regional status
language.pr_citizenship_language_req: Confirmed via UDI (Norwegian Directorate of Immigration): applicants aged 18-67 must pass an oral Norwegian test at B1 or higher, plus either the citizenship test (Statsborgerprøven) or the social-studies test in Norwegian. A2 is accepted only for stateless applicants, refugees/resettled refugees over 55, disability-benefit recipients over 55, or anyone who applied before 1 October 2022. The general residence requirement is 8 years within the last 11. Norway has allowed dual citizenship since 1 January 2020, so naturalizing does not require formally renouncing Iranian citizenship under Norwegian law - Iran's own rules on renunciation are a separate legal question applicants should check independently.

records.reality_paragraph: Norway's Iranian community is the smallest of the three Nordic countries here: Statistics Norway's figures put the Iran-background population (immigrants plus Norway-born children of immigrants combined) at roughly 26,500, heavily concentrated in and around Oslo - real, and with a visible record of political integration (Iranian-Norwegians have reached the presidency of the Storting and other senior roles), but nowhere near Stockholm's critical mass. Oslo's tech and fintech scene is genuinely growing, and salaries are high in absolute terms, which helps offset Norway's famously high cost of living, though it doesn't eliminate it - groceries, restaurants and general consumer prices are among the highest in Europe. Norway's naturalization rules are comparatively more moderate than Denmark's but still substantial (8 years' residence, a B1 oral language test, a citizenship test), and unlike some countries, Norway does not require renouncing an existing citizenship. Income tax is high, as everywhere in the region, but oil-linked public wealth funds an excellent social safety net and public services. As with Sweden and Denmark, the commonly cited expat-survey pattern is that Norwegians are welcoming and fair at work but slower to open up socially outside it, so a real friend group often forms through hobbies, children's schools or a partner's network rather than the workplace. There's no verifiable pattern of discrimination specific to Iranian migrants. The common regret is underestimating the cost of living and the time it takes to build a non-work social life in a small community; the common draw is nature access, high wages, strong family/parental benefits, and a functional, low-drama welfare state.
